paras: The Fayetteville jail watch of 1888 was a confrontation in Fayetteville, North Carolina, in late August 1888, when Black residents gathered at night around the Cumberland County jail holding two Black prisoners accused of assaulting a white woman, and police, white citizens and a militia company dispersed and arrested them. No one was harmed, but the arrested men were bound over to the superior court. White papers treated the affair as an attempted jail delivery and a near 'war of races', while the Charlotte Messenger described it as an effort to protect the prisoners from a rumored lynching.

According to the Fayetteville Observer, two Black men were committed after a hearing in Rockfish township on a charge of 'assault with a deadly weapon upon a white woman' and sent to the Fayetteville jail on a Sunday. A News-Observer dispatch described the charge as an assault on 'a young white lady', and the Messenger later wrote that it was 'a common assault' on a white girl that had been thought indecent. The Observer also recalled that a few weeks earlier a Black crowd had tried to stop officers from jailing several prisoners in the town.

On the following Monday night, about 1:30 or 2 a.m., the jailer found groups of Black men around the jail and sent for the night police. The News-Observer correspondent said they were 'armed with guns, pistols, dirks', and the Observer said they were led by Tom Broadfoot, who had told others to meet him there with arms. Police, white townsmen and magistrate D. Jones disarmed and dispersed them, and three were captured and jailed.

On the Tuesday night Black men again appeared at the jail, and Sheriff Henry C. Fisher had the Fayetteville Independent Light Infantry ready. The soldiers 'made a swoop' and took several more prisoners, and the Observer said two guns were pointed at City Marshal Flowers that night. The Messenger said instead that every Black man found near the jail on the second night was arrested.

The arrested men were tried before magistrates on charges of 'unlawful assembling' or attempting to rescue prisoners and were bound over to the next superior court. The Messenger reported that Broadfoot, James Tucker and English Gee, said elsewhere to have been jailed, had given bail the first night of the trial. No report of the superior court outcome, or of a trial of the two original prisoners, appears in the coverage.

The News-Observer dispatch, reprinted in the Durham Recorder on Aug. 29, praised 'that brave body of soldiers' and called Broadfoot 'an ex-radical office holder' whose conduct 'makes the white men solid for Democracy'. The Fayetteville Observer's article, reprinted by the Henderson Gold Leaf on Sept. 6 under 'White Men, Read', warned of 'negro supremacy' and said Black 'incendiary leaders' would be held responsible for any bloodshed.

The Charlotte Messenger first printed the News-Observer paragraph without comment on Sept. 1 under the heading 'Attempted Jail Delivery'. On Oct. 6, after what it called 'careful inquiry', it rejected the riot story, wrote that 'lynching was freely talked of', and said the men had posted sentinels because they feared the boys 'would be taken from the jail and foully murdered'. The editorial recalled the 'foul murder of Archie Warden on the very steps of the court room in which he was tried', argued that 'the time has come for this lynching to be stopped', and also warned Black residents against 'unlawful action'.

The accounts disagree on whether anyone threatened the prisoners. The Observer called the lynching rumor a pretext and said 'No such threat had been made', while the Messenger reported open talk of lynching and attributed the rumor to 'a drunken white man'. The Messenger itself conceded that 'there was really no danger of the boys being hurt'.

reader.title: Fayetteville jail watch of 1888
bases: The episode turned on a reported fear that two Black prisoners would be taken from the Fayetteville jail and lynched, which Black residents answered by watching the jail (A5, A6); the Observer denied any threat was made (A4).

No one was killed and no mob is reported to have gathered at the jail (A2, A4, A5); the only report of a lynching threat is talk and a rumor said to have been started by a drunken white man (A5, A6), which the Fayetteville Observer denied (A4).

Three independent accounts agree that Black men gathered at the jail on two nights and were arrested (A2, A4, A5), but the Fayetteville Observer says no lynching threat was made (A4) while the Charlotte Messenger says lynching was 'freely talked of' (A5).

accounts.label: News-Observer dispatch
accounts.gist: Armed squads of negroes surrounded the jail on two nights hoping to release the two prisoners; several were captured by citizens, police and soldiers and tried before magistrates.

accounts.label: Fayetteville Observer
accounts.gist: A mob of armed negroes led by Tom Broadfoot occupied the jail grounds using a lynching rumor as a pretext; no lynching threat had been made, and the offenders were bound over to the Superior Court.

accounts.label: Charlotte Messenger's inquiry
accounts.gist: Lynching was freely talked of, so Black residents quietly posted sentinels to guard the two boys; the men arrested were innocent of unlawful assembly, though the paper allowed there was no real danger to the prisoners.

framing.detail: The News-Observer dispatch praised 'that brave body of soldiers' and said the affair 'makes the white men solid for Democracy'.
The Fayetteville Observer, reprinted under 'White Men, Read', warned of 'negro supremacy' and threatened Black 'incendiary leaders' with responsibility for any bloodshed.
The Charlotte Messenger first ran the News-Observer paragraph as 'Attempted Jail Delivery' without comment.
The Messenger's later editorial condemned lynching and defended the Black men as lawful guards of the prisoners, while warning Black residents against 'unlawful action'.
